title: On-call & Incident Response Playbook: Process, Runbooks, Postmortems, Rotations, Game Days, Status & Comms Templates
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Overview

This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical on-call and incident response practices. It covers the incident lifecycle, triage and service runbooks, postmortem process, on-call rotations and responsibilities, game day planning, and ready-made status page and customer communications templates. Use this doc for incident onboarding, live response, and post-incident learning.

Goals
- Restore service as quickly and safely as possible.
- Reduce customer impact through predictable escalation and communication.
- Capture root causes and follow-through action items to prevent recurrence.
- Maintain clear ownership and psychological safety for responders.

Who this applies to
- All on-call engineers and incident responders across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private teams.
- Support engineers and Customer Success for customer-facing communications.

Incident lifecycle (high-level)
1. Detection: Alerting system or external report (customer, sales, monitoring) triggers an incident.
2. Triage: Primary on-call acknowledges and assesses severity within 10 minutes.
3. Mitigation: Apply short-term mitigations (rollbacks, failover, throttling, config changes).
4. Communication: Update internal channels and public status page as appropriate.
5. Recovery: Resume normal operations; verify SLOs returning to normal.
6. Post-incident: Run a blameless postmortem, track action items, and close with follow-up owners.

Severity and SLO thresholds
- Sev 1 / P0: Total or near-total outage for a production-critical surface (e.g., API returns >80% errors, latency >10x SLO). Target acknowledgment: 5 minutes.
- Sev 2 / P1: Major degradation impacting a subset of customers or features (e.g., embeddings failing in one region). Target acknowledgment: 15 minutes.
- Sev 3 / P2: Minor degradation or scheduled maintenance. Target acknowledgment: 1 business day.

SLO examples (for reference)
| Service | Latency SLO (p95) | Error budget | Alert threshold |
| Hosted API (text-gen) | 200ms | 99.9% | p95 > 500ms for 5m or error rate > 2% |
| Embeddings | 150ms | 99.95% | p95 > 400ms or errors > 0.5% |

Pager and escalation matrix (summary)
- Primary on-call (engineer): initial ack and triage.
- Secondary on-call: triage support, deeper debugging.
- Service owner / SME: if root cause requires code or architecture change.
- Eng SRE lead / Manager on-call: for cross-service/regulatory/major incident coordination.
- Exec pager (on-call director): invoked for declared major incidents (customer SLAs breached, regulatory impact).

Contact table (example)
| Role | Pager | Slack channel | Email |
| Primary on-call | Pager rotation | #oncall-primary | oncall+primary@redwood.ai |
| Secondary on-call | Pager rotation | #oncall-secondary | oncall+secondary@redwood.ai |
| Customer Success escalation | N/A | #cs-escalations | cs-esc@redwood.ai |

Triage runbook (step-by-step)
1. Acknowledge the alert (PagerDuty/Datadog) and mark status in Slack (#incident-ops).
2. Gather immediate facts (What, When, Scope, Impact, Initial hypothesis):
   - What is failing? (API endpoints, jobs, nodes)
   - When did it start (first alert timestamp)?
   - Who/which customers are impacted?
   - Any recent deploys/config changes?
3. Assign roles: Incident Commander (IC), Primary Responder, Communicator, Scribe.
4. Run quick mitigation checklist (if applicable):
   - Revert recent deploys (if suspected)
   - Scale up known safe capacity/workers
   - Enable failover routing (region->region)
   - Apply feature flags or throttles to reduce load
5. Verify mitigation effectiveness via metrics and logs.
6. If incident is Sev 1 or customer-impacting, open a Major Incident bridge (Zoom + shared doc).

Service-specific runbook template
Each service must maintain a one-page runbook with:
- Service name and owner
- Key symptoms and dashboards
- Cause hypotheses and known mitigations
- Rolling back and safe deploy guidance
- Contacts and escalation steps

Example runbook snippet (Hosted API core)
- Key dashboards: /dashboards/hosted-text-gen-overview (latency, error-rate, queue length).
- Common symptom: sudden spike in 5xx errors with increased p50 latency.
  - Quick mitigation: redirect a % of traffic to model-variant with known-good runtime (routing policy).
  - If mitigation fails: reduce concurrency settings, increase worker pool size, and contact model-runtime SME.

Communication policy (internal & external)
- Internal: Create #incident-<id> Slack channel. Post summary updates every 15-30 minutes during active mitigation: status, action taken, next steps.
- External: Update status.redwood.ai and customer-facing comms. For Sev 1 incidents, issue a public status update within 30 minutes.
- Avoid speculation; state confirmed facts and known scope.

Status page & customer communications templates
Use the templates below verbatim where appropriate and replace bracketed fields. Maintain tone: factual, empathetic, and concise.

Status page template (initial)
Title: [Service] Partial Outage\Timestamp: [UTC time]\Summary: We are investigating increased errors affecting [feature/region/customers]. Our engineers are actively investigating.\What we're doing: Engineers have identified [initial finding if available]. Short-term mitigations being applied: [e.g., traffic reroute, autoscale].\Customer impact: Some customers may see increased errors or latency for [endpoints].\Next update: We will post another update by [time or within XX minutes].\nStatus page template (update)\Title: [Service] Update — Mitigation in progress\Timestamp: [UTC time]\Summary: Mitigation [describe] is in progress and has reduced error rates from X% to Y%.\Impact: [Updated scope].\Next steps: [e.g., continue monitoring, rollback plan].\nStatus page template (resolved)\Title: [Service] Resolved — [Incident ID]\Timestamp: [UTC time]\Summary: The issue affecting [service] has been resolved. Root cause: [short summary].\Impact: [Customers affected / time window].\Follow-up: A postmortem will be published to customers/internal teams within [72 hours/standard window].\nCustomer support email template (initial)\Subject: Incident affecting [Service] — [Short summary]\Hello [Customer name],\We are investigating an issue affecting [service/feature] that may impact your requests. Our engineering team is actively working on a resolution. We will provide updates via our status page: https://status.redwood.ai and will follow up with more details as they become available.\If you are experiencing a critical business impact, please reply to this email or contact your CSM.\Sincerely,\Redwood Support\(on behalf of Engineering)\nCustomer follow-up email (post-resolution)\Subject: Incident resolved — [Service], [Incident ID]\Hello [Customer name],\We resolved the incident that impacted [service] at [time UTC]. Root cause: [brief root cause]. Mitigation: [what was done]. We are performing follow-up actions and will share the postmortem when complete. If you have any outstanding issues, please let us know.\Sincerely,\Redwood Support

Postmortem process (blameless)
1. Declare a postmortem for any Sev 1 incidents and for Sev 2 incidents with customer impact or systemic root causes.
2. Timeline: Incident declared -> Postmortem draft opened within 48 hours -> Final postmortem published within 72 hours (internal) and 7 days (customer-facing version if needed).
3. Postmortem sections (required):
   - Summary: one-paragraph overview of impact and timeline.
   - Timeline: bulletized, with timestamps (UTC) of key events and actions.
   - Root cause analysis: causal chain and why safeguards failed.
   - Impact: customers, metrics, duration.
   - Action items: specific owners, deadlines, and verification criteria.
   - Follow-up: links to PRs, configs, runbook updates.

Postmortem template snippet
\Title: Postmortem — [Incident ID] — [Service]\Author: [Author]\Severity: [S1/S2]\Summary: [1-3 sentences]\Timeline:
- [UTC timestamp] — [event]\Root cause: [clear causal explanation]\Action items:
- [Action] — owner: [name] — due: [YYYY-MM-DD] — verification: [how we know it’s done]\nRunbook & postmortem ownership\- Every service owner must ensure runbooks and contact lists are up to date after each release.\- Action item owners are responsible for tracking completion in the Eng Platform board and confirming verification steps.

On-call rotations and roles\- Rotation model: 2-week primary on-call shifts with 24/7 coverage, backed by a 2-week secondary rotation. For small teams, rotations may be weekly.\- On-call handover: outgoing on-call must prepare a short handover note in the rotation calendar 1 hour before shift end, listing in-flight incidents and tasks.\- Responsibilities:
  - Primary on-call: triage alerts, lead first mitigation, invoke escalation when needed.\n  - Secondary on-call: support deeper debugging, take over if primary needs context or relief.\n  - On-call backup: scheduled person for planned vacations; not automatically paged unless primary and secondary unavailable.

Handover checklist\- Current incidents and status\- Outstanding action items due during next shift\- Known degradations and scheduled maintenance\- Any experimental flags or risky rollouts in progress

Game days and readiness drills\- Frequency: quarterly team game days and annual cross-team full-stack incident drills.\n- Goals: validate runbooks, verify automated mitigations, test customer comms workflow, measure mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) and mean time to recovery (MTTR).\n- Example game day scenario:
  1. Simulate a model-serving cache invalidation causing spike in latency and errors in Hosted API.\n  2. Measure: Time to detect, time to triage, time to mitigation, time to recovery.\n  3. Outcomes: Update runbook steps that were unclear; fix instrumentation gaps.

Operational tooling & logs\- Incident tracking: PagerDuty for alerting and incident pages.\n- Internal doc: Use the incident-specific Confluence page and incident timeline template.\n- Metrics/logs: Datadog dashboards, OpenSearch logs, and request traces (Honeycomb/Jaeger) must be linked in every incident channel.

Measuring success\- MTTA target: < 5 minutes for Sev 1, < 15 minutes for Sev 2.\- MTTR targets: < 30 minutes for common mitigations, < 4 hours for full recovery on Sev 1.\n- Post-incident closure: All action items assigned and owners identified within 24 hours.

Appendix: Useful commands and quick references\- Rolling back a deployment (example):
  1) kubectl rollout undo deployment/service-api -n prod\ 2) Confirm pods stabilized: kubectl get pods -n prod | grep service-api\- Quick log query (OpenSearch/ELK):
  query: service:hosted-api AND status:[500 TO 599] AND @timestamp:[now-15m TO now]\- Emergency contact escalation policy: If communication to customer success or legal is required, notify Eng SRE lead immediately.
